## merge vs rebase

**merge** — join two branches, keep full history. Creates merge commit.

```
A---B---C  main
     \
      D---E  feature
           \
            M  ← merge commit (has 2 parents)
```

**rebase** — replay feature commits on top of target. Linear history, no merge commit.

```
A---B---C  main
             \
              D'--E'  ← replayed commits (new hashes)
```

---

## When use which

**Use merge when:**
- Public/shared branch (never rewrite shared history)
- Want exact record of when branch integrated
- Team prefers non-destructive workflow

**Use rebase when:**
- Local cleanup before PR
- Want clean linear history
- Updating feature branch with latest main changes

---

## Tradeoffs

| | merge | rebase |
|---|---|---|
| History | Preserves exact truth | Clean but rewritten |
| Conflicts | Resolve once | Resolve per commit |
| Safety | Always safe | Dangerous on shared branches |
| Bisect/log | Noisy | Easy to read |

---

## Golden rule

> **Never rebase commits already pushed to shared branch.**

Rebase rewrites hashes. Others have old hashes. Chaos follows.

---

## Common patterns

```bash
# Update feature branch with main (local only)
git checkout feature
git rebase main

# Merge feature into main (preserves history)
git checkout main
git merge feature

# Interactive rebase: squash messy WIP commits before PR
git rebase -i main
```

**TL;DR:** rebase = clean history, local only. merge = safe, always OK.
